body.statement: Every intensity-optimized clipped-ramp array has fixed potential outcomes bounded by \(M\), deterministic predictable assignment probabilities in \((0,\rho]\), and predictable zero regressions.  Its profiles satisfy \(\bar q_\star\in\mathcal Q\) and \(r^\sigma\in\mathcal R\), and \(r_{nt}(1)=r^\sigma(t/n)\) exactly.  For all sufficiently large \(n\), the propensity cap is inactive simultaneously for every \(t\ge\lceil n\varepsilon_n\rceil\) and every \(t>\lfloor a_\star n\rfloor\); the early rare-arm term and its predictable quadratic variation are zero, and \(G_n=\Omega\).  This is an eventual profile-contract conclusion only: the construction is not asserted to satisfy \(\Pr(G_n)\ge1-\kappa_n\) for every finite \(n\).
body.proof_tex:
The potential outcomes and regressions are deterministic arrays, so they are fixed under assignment.  By construction,
\[
 |Y_{nt}^\sigma(1)|=g_{a_\star}(t/n)\le M,
 \qquad Y_{nt}^\sigma(0)=0,
\]
and the outcome bound follows.  Since \(c/2\le\bar q_\star(u)\le c\) and \(t\ge1\),
\[
 0<e_{nt}=\min\{\rho,\bar q_\star(t/n)/t\}\le\rho<1.
\]
The probabilities are deterministic and hence predictable, and the declared conditional Bernoulli law is a valid adaptive assignment law.  The zero regression is predictable and obeys its bound.

At \(u=0\), \(\bar q_\star(0)=c\).  Also
\[
 c/2\le\bar q_\star(u)\le c\le K.
\]
The functions \(u\mapsto c-L_qu\) and \(u\mapsto c/2\) are respectively \(L_q\)-Lipschitz and constant.  The elementary inequality
\[
 |\max\{x_1,x_2\}-\max\{y_1,y_2\}|
 \le\max\{|x_1-y_1|,|x_2-y_2|\}
\]
therefore shows that \(\bar q_\star\) is \(L_q\)-Lipschitz.  These three facts prove \(\bar q_\star\in\mathcal Q\).  Similarly,
\[
 |r^\sigma(u)|=g_{a_\star}(u)\le M\le B,
\]
and truncating the \(L_r\)-Lipschitz function \(L_r(u-a_\star)_+\) at \(M\) preserves its Lipschitz modulus.  Thus \(r^\sigma\in\mathcal R\).  Because the regression is zero,
\[
 r_{nt}(1)=Y_{nt}^\sigma(1)-m_{nt}(1)=r^\sigma(t/n)
\]
for every \(n,t\).

The conditions \(n\varepsilon_n\to\infty\), \(a_\star>0\), and \(\bar q_\star\le c\) imply that, for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
 \frac{\bar q_\star(t/n)}t\le\frac ct<\rho
\]
both whenever \(t\ge\lceil n\varepsilon_n\rceil\) and whenever \(t>\lfloor a_\star n\rfloor\).  Thus the cap is inactive on both ranges.  On the first range,
\[
 te_{nt}=\bar q_\star(t/n),
\]
so the intensity discrepancy in \(G_n\) is zero, while the residual discrepancy is already zero for every \(n\).

Finally, \(\varepsilon_n+1/n\to0<a_\star\).  Hence eventually every \(t<\lceil n\varepsilon_n\rceil\) satisfies
\[
 t/n<\varepsilon_n+1/n<a_\star,
\]
and therefore \(r_{nt}(1)=0\).  Each summand of the early rare-arm martingale is zero, so both that martingale and its predictable quadratic variation equal zero.  All three clauses defining \(G_n\) then hold identically, proving \(G_n=\Omega\) for sufficiently large \(n\).  No step proves the corresponding assertion at the exceptional finite prefixes, which is why no all-horizon profile-contract membership is claimed.
